claims.text: The patient presented with a severe headache rated 8/10 in intensity, described as sudden 'thunderclap' onset after exertion, throbbing, diffuse, and associated with mild nausea but no vomiting, visual changes, photophobia, or neck stiffness.
The patient reported no past medical history, no current medications, and no known allergies.

Social history indicates the patient lives alone, is independent in daily activities, works as a primary school teacher, engages in regular jogging, denies smoking or recreational drug use, and consumes alcohol in moderation (approximately 6 units per week).
Family history is negative for cerebrovascular accidents, aneurysms, migraines, or neurological conditions; the mother has type 2 diabetes and the father has hypertension.
Initial triage on 2026-01-07 recorded blood pressure at 160/90 mmHg and heart rate at 88 bpm.
Initial neurological examination on 2026-01-07 revealed no abnormalities, with the patient alert, oriented, and having intact cranial nerves, motor, and sensory function.
A CT head scan performed on 2026-01-07 showed no evidence of intracranial hemorrhage, mass lesion, or other abnormalities.
Blood tests collected on 2026-01-07 showed mild leukocytosis (WBC 12.5 x 10^9/L), CRP 8 mg/L, and normal renal and liver function tests.
The patient was admitted to the Neurology ward with a diagnosis of Reversible Cerebral Vasoconstriction Syndrome (RCVS).
On 2026-01-07, the headache persisted at 7/10 intensity, blood pressure was 150/92 mmHg, and blood tests showed mild hypokalemia (K+ 3.3 mmol/L) and marginally elevated CRP (12 mg/L).
MRI/MRA performed on 2026-01-07 confirmed the diagnosis of RCVS.
On 2026-01-08, headache severity reduced to 5/10, blood pressure was 135/85 mmHg, CRP was 12 mg/L, and mild hypokalemia (K+ 3.3 mmol/L) persisted.
On 2026-01-09, headache severity reduced to 3/10, blood pressure was 125/80 mmHg, and blood tests showed mild hyponatremia (Na 132 mmol/L).
On 2026-01-10, headache severity reduced to 2/10, blood pressure was 125/80 mmHg, and mild hyponatremia (Na 132 mmol/L) was noted.
On 2026-01-11, headache severity remained at 2/10, blood pressure was 125/78 mmHg, and a repeat MRA showed significant improvement in cerebral vasoconstriction.
On 2026-01-12, the patient reported no further headaches, blood pressure was 130/80 mmHg, and a repeat MRA confirmed resolution of vasoconstriction.

Medication records conflict regarding the discharge regimen: one source documents nimodipine 30 mg orally every 4 hours to be tapered over 2 weeks, while another source documents amlodipine 5 mg orally once daily.
The patient was discharged on 2026-01-12 with plans for outpatient neurology follow-up in 4 weeks and outpatient physiotherapy to address mild residual neck stiffness.
The patient received education on avoiding triggers such as intense physical exertion, stress, triptans, and ergotamines, and was provided with discharge planning materials.
The GP was contacted on 2026-01-07 and again on 2026-01-12 to provide updates on the admission, diagnosis, and discharge plan.
